title: Quota reservoir sleuthing — notebook
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchbook to record experiments, raw command outputs, and hypotheses around the mysterious quota/reservoir-like 401/429 patterns that pop up for a subset of clients. Not a polished postmortem — just breadcrumbs for triage, tests to reproduce, and next steps.

Summary of observed behavior (high-level):
- Multiple clients across different regions intermittently receive 401 or 429 for short bursts (~30s-2m).
- Pattern often follows a key rotation or a flurry of short-lived ephemeral keys being minted by downstream SDKs.
- Affected clients show no obvious increase in token consumption vs baseline; HTTP headers vary in presence (some responses include Retry-After, others do not).
- Some 401s return a small JSON body citing "invalid_token" while others are plain 401 with no body.

Hypotheses to test: (ranked)
1) Reservoir-style quota: we have a per-key leaky-bucket in front of the control plane that applies cross-client global throttling when certain key patterns are seen.
2) Fingerprint caching: auth cache key uses a derived fingerprint that collisions for ephemeral tokens cause sudden drops.
3) Token issuance timing/race: short-lived keys are issued with clock skew or propagation delay, causing immediate 401 until caches refresh.
4) Edge routing inconsistency: requests hit different edge nodes with differing quota counters or stale auth state.

Repro experiments run so far (commands + raw outputs):
1) Simple burst using curl (target: hosted API /v1/generate endpoint):
$ for i in {1..40}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_KEY" "https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/generate" & done

Observed (sample lines):
200 0.120s
200 0.115s
429 0.012s
200 0.140s
429 0.011s
401 0.009s

Note: 401 appeared only after ~18th concurrent request. Re-ran with same key; behaviour non-deterministic (sometimes no 401).

2) Repro with explicit header echo to capture rate headers:
$ curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_KEY" "https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/status"

Sample response (when 200):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-rate-limit-limit: 120
x-rate-limit-remaining: 117
x-rate-limit-reset: 1670000000
content-type: application/json

Sample 429 response (when hit):
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 10
content-type: application/json
{"error":{"type":"rate_limit","message":"rate limit exceeded"}}

Sample 401 response (when hit):
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
content-type: application/json
{"error":{"type":"invalid_token","message":"token not known"}}

3) Rotation stress test (automated script minted ephemeral keys every 5s and made one request per key):
- Script: rotate-and-call.sh (curl + AWS KMS sign to request ephemeral).
- Observed: roughly 5% of keys immediately returned 401 for the first request, but subsequent attempts with same key succeeded.
- Hypothesis refinement: first-request penalty suggests propagation delay or initial validation path that can fail transiently.

4) Cross-region comparison:
- Ran identical burst from eu-west-1 and us-west-2. eu-west had a higher incidence of 401s but fewer 429s; us-west saw more 429s.
- Suggests different rate window or quota enforcement by region/edge.

What we checked in infra/logs:
- Auth service logs: looked for token-id in invalid_token events; majority show "token not found in cache" and then a subsequent lookup to the issuer returns found.
- Edge logs: some 401s originated at edge with no call to auth service (edge returned 401 for local cache miss).
- Rate limiter telemetry: counters show small bursts of per-key spike followed by rapid decay; no single client exceeded configured per-key limit in telemetry.

Commands used to pull logs (for reference):
$ gcloud logging read "resource.type=gae_app AND textPayload: \"invalid_token\"" --limit 50 --project=redwood-prod --freshness=1h
$ jq -r '.entries[].protoPayload' auth-logs-raw.json | grep "token_id_short" | sed -n '1,120p'

Quick notes on headers we see and their meaning:
- x-rate-limit-limit: configured limit for the window (per-key or per-route)
- x-rate-limit-remaining: tokens left
- x-rate-limit-reset: epoch when window resets
- Retry-After: server hint for backoff (seconds)
- x-auth-cache-hit: (internal) sometimes set to "0" when edge forwarded to auth service

Diagnostic heuristics to differentiate causes:
- If 401s always accompanied by x-auth-cache-hit: 0 -> auth backend not having the token cached (propagation)
- If 401s appear without Retry-After and are isolated -> possibly malformed token or key metadata mismatch
- If 429s have small Retry-After and reduce x-rate-limit-remaining to 0 -> classic rate window crossing

Quick experiments to run next (priority order):
1) First-request reproducibility: issue a brand-new ephemeral key and immediately do N=5 sequential requests from same connection (no parallel). Observe if first fails and subsequent succeed. If so, log time delta between token mint and successful auth.
2) Single-key long-burst vs many short-lived keys: compare 200 requests from one long-lived key vs 200 requests each from 40 ephemeral keys. Measure 401/429 distribution.
3) Inject artificial clock skew on client (set +3m / -3m) to see if token validation window triggers 401s.
4) Pin to single edge node (if possible) to rule out cross-edge inconsistencies.

Temporary mitigations suggested (short-term):
- Add jittered initial backoff (random 100-500ms) on SDKs for first request after key/rotation.
- If issuing ephemeral keys, delay first call by 200-500ms and retry once on 401 before bubbling to user.
- Make SDKs batch rotation events so we don't create many near-simultaneous unique auth primitives.

Notes to share with Auth/Edge teams: (copy/paste to Slack ticket)
"Edge returns transient 401s for ~5% of freshly issued ephemeral keys; logs show edge cache miss then lookup succeeds. Burst patterns of many ephemeral keys correlate with higher 429 incidence. See INF-4923 for traces + repro script. Proposed quick mitigation: SDKs add tiny delay+retry on first key usage, and we investigate reducing cache-pop latency between issuer and edge."

Related tickets & traces to attach:
- INF-4923 (investigation)
- INF-4988 (possible edge cache change)
- sample-traces/ephemeral-rotation-2026-02-25.json (upload pending to ticket)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is there any per-API-key global reservoir that can silently borrow capacity from similar keys? (I think not, but telemetry alignment needed.)
- Are there any downstream CDNs or WAFs that could be interfering and returning 401 before edge?
- Is the auth issuer publishing token IDs to an eventually-consistent store that has noticeable propagation lag?

Housekeeping / next actions for me (Maggie):
- [ ] Run prioritized experiments (first-request, single-vs-many) and capture header-level traces.
- [ ] Add short experiment script to repo: infra/auth/repro/ephemeral-burst-test.sh
- [ ] Sync with @Ravi (edge) and ask for a wall-clock aligned trace view for the timestamps in INF-4923
- [ ] Draft short note for SDKs team recommending small first-request backoff and single immediate retry on 401

If someone else picks this up, start with the rotation stress test log (trace id: trace-ephem-20260225-1) and repro with a controlled process that logs every token-id, issuance time, and first-request time.

Raw snippets (copyable):
- curl burst example:
for i in {1..80}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_KEY" "https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/generate" & done

- sample 401 body to mimic in tests:
{"error":{"type":"invalid_token","message":"token not known"}}

- recommended tiny-backoff pseudo: sleep $((RANDOM%400+100))/1000  # 100-500ms jitter before first call

End of notebook.
